steps.action:
# How a Transformer Works (Conceptually)

## The Core Problem
Transformers process sequences (words, tokens) and need to understand **how each element relates to every other element** — regardless of distance.

---

## Key Mechanisms

### 1. Tokenization & Embeddings
- Input text is split into tokens
- Each token becomes a vector (list of numbers) representing its meaning
- **Positional encoding** is added so the model knows *order*

### 2. Self-Attention — The Heart of It
For each token, the model asks:
> *"Which other tokens should I pay attention to when understanding this one?"*

Each token generates three vectors:
- **Query** — "what am I looking for?"
- **Key** — "what do I offer?"
- **Value** — "what information do I carry?"

Attention scores are computed by matching Queries against Keys, then used to weight the Values. Every token can "look at" every other token simultaneously.

### 3. Multi-Head Attention
Run self-attention **multiple times in parallel** (different "heads"), each learning different relationship types (syntax, coreference, semantics, etc.)

### 4. Feed-Forward Layers
After attention, each token passes through a small neural network independently — adding computational depth.

### 5. Layer Stacking
Repeat attention + feed-forward **many times** (e.g., 12–96 layers), building increasingly abstract representations.

---

## Why It Was Revolutionary
| Old (RNNs) | Transformers |
|---|---|
| Processed sequentially | Processes all tokens in parallel |
| Struggled with long-range dependencies | Handles them directly via attention |
| Slow to train | Much faster to train |

---

## The Big Intuition
A transformer lets **every word vote on the meaning of every other word**, simultaneously, across many layers — building rich contextual understanding.
